newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ monetary conditions loosen as debt mkts rally.
newsitem.headline: NZ monetary conditions loosen as debt mkts rally.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.99 (PREV 93.02) 90-DAYS 7.01 (PREV 7.00)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.85 PCT (PREV 6.85) US 5-YR 6.49 (PREV 6.49)
NZ MCI vs -0.96 vs -0.90
* NZ bank bills ease only a touch on lower TWI
* NZ monetary conditions now very loose
* Market poised for possible RBNZ action
* Shortage of Govt stock supply sees bonds rally
New Zealand debt markets were on edge at the open on Friday as anticipation grew that the Reserve Bank could take action to correct severely loose monetary conditions.
"If the market doesn't do something to correct itself in the opening stages, then the Reserve Bank may come out and say something," a dealer said.
A shortage of government stock has kept the yield curve well bid despite the currency's Trade-Weighted Index shedding more than 30 points since Thursday's open.
That has seen monetary conditions loosen to what some in the amrket call dangerous levels, the Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) falling deep into the negative nineties.
"I think the main focus of attention is going to be the MCI. It's at dangerous levels now and the feeling is that the Reserve Bank may in fact act," the dealer said.

The 90-day bank bill rate was just a point higher at 7.01 percent in the face of the sharply lower TWI. But a shortage of supply in the bond market pushed yields down seven to eight points across the curve, with the 02/00s rallying to 6.95 percent and the 11/06s to 7.25 percent in early trade.
A NZ$100 million three-year Eurobond issued by the World Bank overnight was indicative of the high demand for New Zealand assets, dealers said.
"People are ignoring monetary conditions, there are other factors pressuring the market at the moment," said a senior bond dealer.
He said the market would love the Reserve Bank to come out and push the market back, but the shortage of supply seemed to leave the bank "in a bit of a bind".
"I can't see any move by the RB backing the market up. I think the market's waiting for that so they can buy it, but who's going to sell it?"
"We just haven't go the assets here at the moment."
He said bond yields could fall by another five basis points this session.
-- Matthew Brockett, Wellington newsroom +64 4 473-3736
